rv.q: But from this point the play becomes diffuse, a quilt of underdeveloped subplots.

That's the peculiar premise of "Her Requiem," Greg Pierce's well-written but ineffectual play about a teenage wunderkind whose miraculous musical genius turns her home life upside-down and inspires a morbid death cult.
Contrived and gently pretentious, Greg Pierce's Her Requiem is the Off Broadway equivalent of a New Yorker short story.
When, at the end, several of the characters sit down to listen to the opening moments of Caitlin’s composition, it feels like the requiem should be for the play itself.
Pierce probingly explores our tendency to see our own issues in a great works of art, even if those themes weren't intended by the artist.
If this may (or may not) be catnip for classically trained musicians, it is hard to imagine anybody else leaving “My Requiem” and rushing to set up a requiem playlist.

A highbrow variation of the old stage-mother scenario, Her Requiem has some interesting ideas that haven't quite coalesced yet, but with Winningham and Friedman at the center, the 90-minute piece certainly intrigues.
Although Keilly McQuail gives a nuanced performance as the Goth in charge of the never-seen kids sleeping in the barn, their place in the story feels awkward and unnecessary.
Her Requiem is ambitious but it both overpromises and underperforms.

cn.t: Pierce's family drama about a teenage musical prodigy earns praise for strong performances and thoughtful themes, but critics find the premise improbable and the execution uneven, with the focus oddly shifting from daughter to father.
